title: Why Do Crabs Walk Sideways? (8 Legs, 1 Hinge) 🦀
description:
Why do crabs walk sideways? A crab's wide, flat body stiffens its shoulder joints, so its legs bend at a simple hinge that only swings out to the side, which makes sideways scuttling far faster than shuffling forward, and a 2026 study of 50 crab species suggests the trick evolved just once, about 200 million years ago.

script: Why do crabs walk sideways? You'd never guess it's their knees. A crab's body is wide and flat, perfect for squeezing under rocks. But that shape stiffens its shoulder joints. So the real bending happens one joint down, a simple hinge, like your knee, that only swings out to the side. Eight walking legs, all hinged that way. Going forward, a crab can only shuffle. Sideways, those hinges swing wide, and it zooms. It can dart left or right in a flash, so a hungry gull can't guess where it's going. Scientists filmed fifty kinds of crabs. Thirty-five of them walked sideways. They think the trick showed up just once, about two hundred million years ago. So if your knees bent sideways, where would you scuttle first?
key_facts: A crab's wide, flat body restricts the shoulder joint of each leg (BBC Science Focus)
The second leg joint is a simple hinge, like a knee, that only bends sideways, so sideways walking is much faster (BBC Science Focus)
Crabs have eight walking legs plus two claws
Taniguchi et al. (eLife 2026) filmed 50 true crab species: 35 moved mainly sideways, 15 forward
Sideways walking likely evolved once, about 200 million years ago, at the base of Eubrachyura
Moving sideways lets crabs dart either way, making their path harder for predators to predict
